sections.title: Start here
sections.body:
Surveying turns measurements on the ground into positions, areas, volumes and elevations. Angles and distances give horizontal position. A level and a rod give height.

Most questions are careful bookkeeping: add and subtract in the right order and keep track of direction.
pitfalls: Swapping backsight and foresight. Backsight is added to the known elevation and foresight is subtracted.
Mixing bearings and azimuths without converting.

tips.from: Mark Mattson, FE Surveying Review Session 2022
items: A direction between two points is the inverse tangent of the change in easting over the change in northing; then fix the quadrant.
In the coordinate method for area, close the figure by returning to the first point.
The trapezoidal rule and Simpson's rule give slightly different areas from the same offsets; use the one the question names.
Average end area is the three-dimensional version of the trapezoid: mean of the two end areas times the distance between them.

bridge.plain: Surveying measures where things are: distances, directions, elevations, areas and volumes of earth.
core: A direction is an angle from north.
A line can be split into a north-south part and an east-west part.
Elevations are carried from a known point by reading a rod through a level.
Earthwork volume is cross-section area times distance.
bridge.links: It is applied trigonometry. Road geometry in transportation and quantities in construction use its results.
bridge.exam: The exam expects the hand method: set out a small table and fill it in.

sections.title: Angles, distances and trigonometry
sections.body:
Surveying measures angles and distances and turns them into positions. Directions are written two ways. An azimuth is one angle from 0° to 360°, clockwise from north. A bearing is an angle up to 90° from north or south toward east or west, such as S 35° W.

Distances measured along a slope must be reduced to horizontal. The interior angles of a closed traverse with n sides should add to (n - 2) × 180°; the shortfall or excess is the misclosure and is spread among the angles.
pitfalls: Measuring a bearing from the east-west line. Bearings are always from north or south.

example.problem: Convert an azimuth of 200° to a bearing.
example.steps:
200° is 20° past south, on the west side.

Bearing = S 20° W.

ideas.title: Reversing a bearing
ideas.text: Travelling the other way along a line keeps the angle and swaps both letters: N 30° E becomes S 30° W.

ideas.title: Degrees, minutes and seconds
ideas.text: Decimal degrees = degrees + minutes / 60 + seconds / 3,600.

ideas.title: The compass rule
ideas.text: A closed traverse's latitudes and departures should each sum to zero. Share the misclosure among the legs in proportion to their lengths: correction = -(misclosure) × (leg length / perimeter), done separately for latitude and departure.

ideas.title: Deflection angle to the end of a curve
ideas.text: Standing at the PC and sighting the PI, the angle turned to the PT is half the intersection angle.

ideas.title: Trigonometry
ideas.text: A slope measurement is the hypotenuse of a right triangle. The horizontal distance is the slope distance times the cosine of the vertical angle, and the elevation difference is the slope distance times the sine.

ideas.title: Regular polygon
ideas.text: The interior angles of any closed polygon with n sides sum to (n - 2) × 180°. Comparing the measured sum with this value gives the angular misclosure of a traverse.

ideas.title: Trigonometry
ideas.text: A degree has 60 minutes and a minute has 60 seconds, so decimal degrees = degrees + minutes / 60 + seconds / 3,600.

ideas.title: Latitude
ideas.text: The compass rule shares the misclosure among the legs in proportion to their lengths, with the opposite sign so that the corrected latitudes sum to zero.

examples.problem: A slope distance of 412.60 m is measured at a vertical angle of 9° above horizontal. What is the horizontal distance?
examples.idea: A slope measurement is the hypotenuse of a right triangle. The horizontal distance is the slope distance times the cosine of the vertical angle, and the elevation difference is the slope distance times the sine.

examples.problem: What should the interior angles of a closed seven-sided traverse add up to?
examples.idea: The interior angles of any closed polygon with n sides sum to (n - 2) × 180°. Comparing the measured sum with this value gives the angular misclosure of a traverse.

examples.problem: Convert 74° 12' 45" to decimal degrees.
examples.idea: A degree has 60 minutes and a minute has 60 seconds, so decimal degrees = degrees + minutes / 60 + seconds / 3,600.

examples.problem: A closed traverse has a perimeter of 960 m and a misclosure in latitude of 0.16 m. Using the compass rule, what correction is applied to the latitude of a 240.0 m leg?
examples.idea: The compass rule shares the misclosure among the legs in proportion to their lengths, with the opposite sign so that the corrected latitudes sum to zero.

examples.problem: A steel tape, correct at 20 °C, is used to measure 302 m at 24 °C. The coefficient of thermal expansion of steel is 11.6 × 10^{-6} per °C. What correction should be applied to the measured length?
examples.idea: A warm tape is longer than its marks say, so it reads short and the correction is positive; a cold tape reads long and the correction is negative. The size is (coefficient)(temperature difference)(length).

sections.deep:
Surveying measurements are angles and distances, reduced with trigonometry. Directions are stated as azimuths, measured clockwise from north from 0° to 360°, or as bearings, an acute angle from north or south toward east or west. Each line of a traverse has a latitude, L cos(azimuth), and a departure, L sin(azimuth).

In a closed traverse the latitudes and departures should each sum to zero. What is left is the misclosure, and its length divided by the perimeter gives the precision. Slope distances are reduced to horizontal with the cosine of the vertical angle.
method: Convert every bearing to an azimuth or keep careful track of signs.
Compute latitude and departure for each line.
Sum them; for a closed figure the sums are the misclosures.
Compute the linear misclosure as the square root of the sum of squares, and precision as misclosure over perimeter.
Reduce slope distances to horizontal before anything else.

sections.primer: Survey measurements are distances and angles. A direction is given as an azimuth (an angle clockwise from north) or a bearing (an angle from north or south toward east or west). Sloping distances are converted to horizontal ones with trigonometry.
terms: a direction given as an angle measured clockwise from north, from 0° to 360°
the north-south component of a survey line
the east-west component of a survey line

sections.title: Area computations
sections.body:
Land area is computed from the coordinates of the corners or from measured offsets. The coordinate method cross-multiplies around the boundary and halves the result. For irregular boundaries, offsets measured at regular intervals are summed by the trapezoidal rule or Simpson's rule.

A triangle's area follows from two sides and the included angle, or from all three sides. Areas are often wanted in hectares (10,000 m^{2}) or acres (43,560 ft^{2}).
pitfalls: Listing the corners out of order around the boundary.
Forgetting to halve the cross-multiplied sum.
Leaving an area in square feet when acres are asked for. Divide by 43,560.

example.problem: Find the area of a triangle with corners at (0, 0), (40, 0) and (0, 30) metres.

figure.caption: Area by coordinates: list the corners in order and apply the cross-product sum.

ideas.title: A way to remember the coordinate method
ideas.text: List the corners in order with the first repeated at the end. Multiply each x by the next y and add; multiply each y by the next x and add; subtract and halve.

ideas.title: Simpson's 1/3 rule
ideas.text: It needs an odd number of offsets, which is an even number of intervals. Area = (interval / 3) × (first + last + 4 × the even-numbered offsets + 2 × the odd-numbered interior ones).

ideas.title: Area by coordinates
ideas.text: The area of a closed polygon from corner coordinates is half the absolute value of the sum of the cross products x_{i} y_{i+1} - x_{i+1} y_{i} taken around the boundary (the coordinate or shoelace method).

ideas.title: Trigonometry
ideas.text: When two sides and the included angle are known, area = (1/2) a b sin(C). The term b sin(C) is the height of the triangle measured from side a.

ideas.title: Trapezoidal rule
ideas.text: The trapezoidal rule treats each strip between adjacent offsets as a trapezoid. Summed, the area is the common interval times (half the first and last offsets plus all the offsets in between). Simpson's 1/3 rule fits parabolas instead and needs an even number of intervals.

examples.problem: A four-sided parcel has corners, in order, at (0, 0), (70, 0), (100, 60) and (20, 80), with coordinates in metres. What is its area?
examples.idea: The area of a closed polygon from corner coordinates is half the absolute value of the sum of the cross products x_{i} y_{i+1} - x_{i+1} y_{i} taken around the boundary (the coordinate or shoelace method).

examples.problem: A triangular parcel has sides of 72, 98 and 118 m. What is its area?
examples.idea: With three sides known and no angles, use Heron's formula: area = square root of s(s - a)(s - b)(s - c), where s is half the perimeter.

examples.problem: A rectangular lot measures 434.4 ft by 269.4 ft. What is its area in acres?
examples.idea: An acre is 43,560 square feet. Work out the area in square feet, then divide.

sections.deep:
Areas of land parcels are found from coordinates or from offsets. The coordinate method works for any closed polygon: half the absolute value of the sum of cross products of successive corners. For a boundary that curves, offsets measured at regular intervals from a baseline are combined with the trapezoidal rule or, for an even number of intervals, Simpson's 1/3 rule, which is more accurate.

Simple figures use geometry directly: half the base times the height, or half the product of two sides and the sine of the included angle.
method: List the corners in order around the figure and repeat the first at the end.
Compute each x_{i} y_{i+1} - x_{i+1} y_{i} and add them.
Halve the absolute value.
For offsets, apply the trapezoidal or Simpson's rule with the common interval.
Convert units if asked: 1 acre = 43,560 ft^{2}; 1 hectare = 10,000 m^{2}.

sections.primer: The area of a parcel can be found from the coordinates of its corners, from its sides and angles, or, for a curved edge, by adding up strips measured at regular spacing.
symbols: angle between the two known sides
half the perimeter of the triangle

sections.title: Earthwork and volume computations
sections.body:
Earthwork volume is found from cross-sections cut along the route. The average end area method multiplies the mean of two neighbouring cross-section areas by the distance between them. It slightly overestimates when the sections differ a lot. The prismoidal formula is more exact because it also uses the middle section.

For pits and building sites, a grid of cut depths gives volume as plan area times average depth. Soil swells when dug and shrinks when compacted, so bank, loose and compacted volumes differ.
pitfalls: Adding cut and fill together. Keep them separate.
Reporting cubic feet when cubic yards are asked for. Divide by 27.

example.problem: Stations 30 m apart have fill areas of 18 m^{2} and 26 m^{2}. Find the fill volume.

ideas.title: The prismoidal formula
ideas.text: V = L (A_{1} + 4 A_{m} + A_{2}) / 6, where A_{m} is the area of the section midway between the ends. It is a weighted average that counts the middle four times, and it is exact for a true prismoid. Average end area gives a slightly larger volume.

ideas.title: Borrow pits
ideas.text: For each grid cell, volume is the plan area times the mean of its corner depths. Add the cells.

ideas.title: Average end area
ideas.text: The average end area method treats the earthwork between two cross-sections as a prism whose cross-section is the mean of the two end areas: V = L (A_{1} + A_{2}) / 2. It slightly overestimates when the areas differ a lot.

ideas.title: Earthwork formulas
ideas.text: Borrow pit volume is plan area times average depth of cut. On a grid, the average depth is found by weighting each corner depth by the number of grid squares it touches.

ideas.title: Prismoidal formula
ideas.text: The prismoidal formula is a weighted average of three sections: each end once and the middle four times, divided by six. It is exact for a prismoid, and the average end area method gives a slightly larger volume.

examples.problem: Two road cross-sections 30 m apart have cut areas of 28 m^{2} and 44 m^{2}. Using the average end area method, what is the volume of cut between them?
examples.idea: The average end area method treats the earthwork between two cross-sections as a prism whose cross-section is the mean of the two end areas: V = L (A_{1} + A_{2}) / 2. It slightly overestimates when the areas differ a lot.

examples.problem: A borrow pit measures 30 m by 45 m in plan. Its average depth of cut is 2.2 m. What volume is excavated?
examples.idea: Borrow pit volume is plan area times average depth of cut. On a grid, the average depth is found by weighting each corner depth by the number of grid squares it touches.

examples.problem: Two end sections of a cut are 50 m apart, with areas of 16 m^{2} and 30 m^{2}. The section midway between them has an area of 22 m^{2}. Using the prismoidal formula, what is the volume?
examples.idea: The prismoidal formula is a weighted average of three sections: each end once and the middle four times, divided by six. It is exact for a prismoid, and the average end area method gives a slightly larger volume.

examples.problem: An embankment needs 6,400 m^{3} of compacted fill. The borrow material shrinks by 12% when compacted. What bank volume must be excavated from the borrow pit?
examples.idea: Soil compacted in a fill usually occupies less volume than it did in the ground. Divide the compacted volume by (1 - shrinkage) to find the bank volume needed.

examples.problem: A roadway cut on level ground has a base width of 8.8 m, a centreline depth of 2.5 m and side slopes of 2.2 horizontal to 1 vertical. What is the cross-sectional area of the cut?
examples.idea: A level section is a trapezoid: the base width plus a triangle on each side whose width is the side slope times the depth. Area = d(b + s d).

examples.problem: A conical stockpile of aggregate has a base diameter of 24 m and a height of 6.8 m. What is its volume?
examples.idea: The volume of a cone is one third of the base area times the height.

sections.deep:
Earthwork volumes come from cross-sections taken at stations along the alignment. The average end area method multiplies the mean of two adjacent areas by the distance between them. The prismoidal formula adds the middle area with a weight of four and is more exact.

Borrow pits are computed from a grid of cut depths, weighting each corner by the number of squares it touches. Soil changes volume when moved: it swells when excavated and shrinks when compacted, so bank, loose and compacted volumes differ. A mass diagram plots cumulative cut minus fill to plan hauling.
method: Compute or read the end areas at each station.
Apply average end area between each pair and sum along the alignment.
Keep cut and fill separate.
Apply swell or shrinkage factors to convert between bank, loose and compacted volumes.
Watch stationing: one full station is 100 ft or, in metric practice, commonly 1 km with decimals.

sections.primer: Earthwork is measured from cross-sections drawn at intervals along a route. The volume between two sections is roughly their average area times the distance between them. Soil also changes volume when it is dug up and when it is compacted.
sections.work: Cut and fill quantities on a road project come from end areas at each cross-section.
symbols: area of the first end section
area of the second end section
area of the section midway between the ends

sections.title: Coordinate systems
sections.body:
Positions are recorded as northings and eastings on a plane grid, such as a state plane system, or as latitude and longitude on the curved earth. State plane coordinates flatten a zone of the earth so that ordinary plane geometry works within small errors.

Each traverse line has a latitude (its north-south part) and a departure (its east-west part). Add them to the coordinates of the starting point to get the next point. In a closed traverse the latitudes and the departures should each add to zero; what is left is the error of closure.
pitfalls: Swapping sine and cosine: with azimuths from north, cosine gives the north part.

example.problem: A line runs 150 m at an azimuth of 120°. Find its latitude and departure.
example.steps:
Latitude = 150 cos 120° = -75.0 m (south).

Departure = 150 sin 120° = 129.9 m (east).

ideas.title: State plane coordinates
ideas.text: Each state is divided into zones, and each zone uses its own map projection to give northings and eastings on a flat grid. The projection introduces a small, known scale distortion, and a zone is not meant for mapping across states.

ideas.title: Latitude
ideas.text: Azimuth is measured clockwise from north. Latitude (the north-south component) is L cos(azimuth) and departure (the east-west component) is L sin(azimuth). East and north are positive.

ideas.title: Latitude
ideas.text: A bearing of S (angle) E points south and east, so the line's latitude is negative and its departure is positive. The new northing is the old northing plus the latitude, where latitude = -L cos(bearing angle).

ideas.title: Latitude
ideas.text: The direction between two coordinated points comes from the differences in easting and northing: tan(azimuth) = change in easting / change in northing. The signs of the two differences fix the quadrant, so add 180° or 360° to the calculator result when the line does not run north-east.

examples.problem: A traverse line is 264.50 m long with an azimuth of 48°. What is its departure (east-west component)?
examples.idea: Azimuth is measured clockwise from north. Latitude (the north-south component) is L cos(azimuth) and departure (the east-west component) is L sin(azimuth). East and north are positive.
examples.steps:
Departure = L sin(azimuth) = 264.50 × sin 48° = 196.6 m (east).

Latitude = 264.50 × cos 48° = 177.0 m (north).

examples.problem: Point A has a northing of 3,200.00 m and an easting of 500.00 m. Point B is 145.00 m from A on a bearing of S 35° E. What is the northing of B?
examples.idea: A bearing of S (angle) E points south and east, so the line's latitude is negative and its departure is positive. The new northing is the old northing plus the latitude, where latitude = -L cos(bearing angle).
examples.steps:
Latitude = -145.00 × cos 35° = -118.78 m.

Northing of B = 3,200.00 - 118.78 = 3,081.22 m.

For reference, easting of B = 500.00 + 145.00 sin 35° = 583.17 m.

examples.problem: Point A has coordinates N 800.00, E 600.00 and point B has coordinates N 1,150.00, E 1,500.00, in metres. What is the azimuth of the line from A to B?
examples.idea: The direction between two coordinated points comes from the differences in easting and northing: tan(azimuth) = change in easting / change in northing. The signs of the two differences fix the quadrant, so add 180° or 360° to the calculator result when the line does not run north-east.
examples.steps:
Change in northing = 1,150.00 - 800.00 = 350.00 m. Change in easting = 1,500.00 - 600.00 = 900.00 m. Both are positive, so the line runs north-east.

Azimuth = arctan(\frac{900.00}{350.00}) = 68.75°.

Length = \sqrt{350.00^{2} + 900.00^{2}} = 965.66 m.

examples.problem: Point A is at N 3,035.20, E 2,280.10 and point B is at N 3,005.20, E 2,407.60, in metres. What is the horizontal distance from A to B?
examples.idea: The difference in northings is the latitude of the line and the difference in eastings is its departure. The distance is the hypotenuse.

examples.problem: A closed traverse 1,000 m long has a misclosure of 0.036 m in latitude and 0.058 m in departure. Its relative precision is 1 in N. What is N?
examples.idea: The linear misclosure is the hypotenuse of the latitude and departure misclosures. Relative precision is the perimeter divided by that misclosure, written as 1 in N.

examples.problem: A ground distance of 1,732.88 m is to be reduced to the state plane grid. The combined scale factor is 1.00002. What is the grid distance?
examples.idea: State plane coordinates lie on a projection surface. The combined factor allows for both the elevation of the ground above the ellipsoid and the scale of the projection at that place: grid = ground × combined factor.

sections.deep:
A coordinate system fixes every point by a northing and an easting. Moving from a known point along a line adds the line's latitude to the northing and its departure to the easting. Going the other way, the differences in coordinates between two points give the distance by the Pythagorean theorem and the direction by the inverse tangent of the easting difference over the northing difference.

State plane coordinates extend this idea over a whole region with a map projection. Stationing measures distance along an alignment, written as full stations plus a remainder.
method: Sketch the two points and the north arrow.
Compute the differences in northing and easting.
Distance is the square root of the sum of squares.
Azimuth is the inverse tangent of easting difference over northing difference, placed in the correct quadrant from the signs.
To set out a point, reverse the steps with latitude and departure.
sections.credit: Some of the points in this lesson follow Mark Mattson's 2022 FE review session for this topic, restated in this site's words.
sections.primer: A coordinate system gives every point a northing and an easting. Moving along a line changes them by the line's north-south part (latitude) and east-west part (departure), found from its length and direction.
terms: the north-south component of a survey line
the east-west component of a survey line
a direction given as an angle measured clockwise from north, from 0° to 360°
symbols: denominator of the relative precision, 1 in N; in other questions, northing

sections.title: Leveling
sections.body:
Leveling finds elevations with a level and a graduated rod. The instrument gives a horizontal line of sight. A backsight on a point of known elevation gives the height of the instrument. A foresight on a new point is subtracted to give its elevation.

Carry elevations forward through turning points and close on a known benchmark to check the work. Grade is rise over run, usually as a percent.
pitfalls: Adding the foresight instead of subtracting it.

example.problem: From a benchmark at 50.00 m, the backsight is 2.10 m and the foresight on point A is 0.85 m. Find the elevation of A.

figure.alt: A level set up between a benchmark and a new point, with a backsight of 1.52 m and a foresight of 2.31 m.
figure.caption: Differential leveling: height of instrument = benchmark + backsight; new elevation = height of instrument - foresight.

ideas.title: Trigonometric leveling
ideas.text: With a total station, the elevation difference is the slope distance times the sine of the vertical angle, or the cosine of the zenith angle. If the same prism height is used on both shots it cancels.

Differential leveling: the height of instrument is the benchmark elevation plus the backsight. The elevation of the new point is the height of instrument minus the foresight. A larger foresight means lower ground.
Grade is rise over horizontal run, expressed as a percentage. It is positive going uphill in the direction of stationing.

examples.problem: A level is set up between a benchmark at elevation 75.50 m and a new point. The backsight reading on the benchmark is 1.84 m and the foresight reading on the new point is 2.96 m. What is the elevation of the new point?
examples.idea: Differential leveling: the height of instrument is the benchmark elevation plus the backsight. The elevation of the new point is the height of instrument minus the foresight. A larger foresight means lower ground.
examples.steps:
Height of instrument = 75.50 + 1.84 = 77.34 m.

Elevation = 77.34 - 2.96 = 74.38 m.

figure.alt: A level set up between a benchmark and a new point, with a backsight of 1.84 m and a foresight of 2.96 m.

examples.problem: A road rises from elevation 150.0 m to elevation 162.6 m over a horizontal distance of 360 m. What is the grade?
examples.idea: Grade is rise over horizontal run, expressed as a percentage. It is positive going uphill in the direction of stationing.

examples.problem: A level run starts on a benchmark at 129.03 m. The readings are: backsight 1.475, foresight 1.791 on a turning point, then backsight 1.598 on the turning point and foresight 2.130 on the new point. What is the new point's elevation?
examples.idea: Each set-up adds the backsight to get the height of instrument and subtracts the foresight to get the next elevation. Over the whole run, elevation = start + sum of backsights - sum of foresights.

examples.problem: Using c = 0.0675 K^{2}, with c in metres and K in kilometres, what is the combined correction for earth curvature and refraction on a level sight 1.6 km long?
examples.idea: Over a long sight the level surface curves away below the line of sight, while refraction bends the line slightly back down. The combined effect grows with the square of the distance, which is why backsight and foresight distances are kept equal.

examples.problem: A profile grade line passes through elevation 196.57 m and runs at a grade of 2.9%. What is its elevation 352 m farther along?
examples.idea: A grade in percent is metres of rise per 100 m of run; a negative grade falls. Elevation change = grade / 100 × distance.

examples.problem: A total station with a height of instrument of 1.55 m measures a slope distance of 101.2 m at a vertical angle of +7.62° to a prism on a 1.39 m rod. How much higher is the ground at the rod than the ground at the instrument?
examples.idea: The vertical component of the slope distance is S sin(vertical angle). Add the instrument height, because the measurement starts above the ground, and subtract the rod height, because it ends above the ground.

sections.deep:
Differential leveling carries elevation from a benchmark to new points with a level and a rod. The backsight on a point of known elevation gives the height of the instrument; subtracting the foresight on the new point gives its elevation. Turning points link successive setups.

A level circuit that returns to its start, or ends on another benchmark, shows its error as the misclosure, which is distributed in proportion to the number of setups or the distance. Over long sights the curvature of the earth and refraction matter; balancing backsight and foresight distances cancels them.
method: Start with the benchmark elevation.
Add the backsight to get the height of instrument.
Subtract the foresight to get the new elevation.
Repeat through each turning point.
Check: sum of backsights minus sum of foresights equals last elevation minus first.
sections.credit: Some of the points in this lesson follow Mark Mattson's 2022 FE review session for this topic, restated in this site's words.
sections.primer: Levelling finds elevations. A level gives a horizontal line of sight; reading a rod on a known point and then on a new point gives the difference in height. A grade is the rise or fall per hundred units of distance.
leads: Construction Engineering: Interpretation of engineering drawings
terms: a level-rod reading taken on a point of known elevation
a level-rod reading taken on a point whose elevation is wanted
symbols: combined correction for earth curvature and refraction
